items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+34}}\, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
As it is, this integral doesn't resemble any of the basic integrals we have encountered so far. However, we can complete the square for the denominator, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − 10x + 34|= x^{2} − 10x + (25 − 25) + 34; = (x^{2} − 10x + 25) − 25 + 34; = (x − 5)^{2} + 9]

Content:
If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of [MATH: 9] in the denominator, we get

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(x^{2} − 10x + 34))dx|= ∫(1)/(sqrt((x − 5)^{2} + 9))dx; = ∫(1)/(sqrt(9[((x − 5)^{2})/(9) + 1]))dx; = (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(((x − 5)/(3))^{2} + 1))dx.]

Content:
This now looks more familiar! Let [MATH: u = \dfrac {x-5}{3}.] Then

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u.]

Content:
We can now write the integral as

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(x^{2} − 10x + 34))dx|= (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(((x − 5)/(3))^{2} + 1))dx; = (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1)) ⋅ (3du); = ∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1))du.]

Content:
This is a basic integral for an inverse hyperbolic function, and we can solve it in one step:

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1))du|= arsinh u + C; = arsinh ((x − 5)/(3)) + C]

items.title: Computing an Inverse Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note that [MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{\left(x - 1\right)^2-9}} = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{9\left(\dfrac{x - 1}{3}\right)^2-9}} = \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left( \dfrac{x-1}{3}\right)^2-1}} \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u =\dfrac{x-1}{3}.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore, [MATH: (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(((x − 1)/(3))^{2} − 1))dx|= (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1)) ⋅ 3du; = arcosh u + C; = arcosh ((x − 1)/(3)) + C.]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{\left(x - 1\right)^2-9}}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we note that
[MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{\left(x - 1\right)^2-9}}
= \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{9\left(\dfrac{x - 1}{3}\right)^2-9}}
= \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left( \dfrac{x-1}{3}\right)^2-1}} \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u =\dfrac{x-1}{3}.] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,
[MATH: (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(((x − 1)/(3))^{2} − 1))dx|= (1)/(3)∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1)) ⋅ 3du; = arcosh u + C; = arcosh ((x − 1)/(3)) + C.]

items.title: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcsine Integral

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: [MATH: \eqalign{ x^2-2x+2 & = x^2 - 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 + 2 \[3pt] &= (x-1)^2 -1+2 \[3pt] &= (x-1)^2 + 1 }] Substituting the above into the given integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt{x^2-2x+2}} = \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\sqrt { (x-1)^2 + 1}}.]

Let [MATH: u = x-1.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∫(dx)/(sqrt(x^{2} − 2x + 2))|= ∫(dx)/(sqrt((x − 1)^{2} + 1)); = ∫(du)/(sqrt(u^{2} + 1)); = arsinh u + C; = arsinh (x − 1) + C.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

[MATH: x^{2} − 4x + 3|= x^{2} − 2 ⋅ 2x + 2^{2} − 2^{2} + 3; = (x − 2)^{2} − 1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^2-4x+3}} \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{2}{\sqrt {(x-2)^2-1} } \, \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x-2.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∫(2)/(sqrt(x^{2} − 4x + 3))dx|= ∫(2)/(sqrt((x − 2)^{2} − 1))dx; = 2∫(1)/(sqrt(u^{2} − 1))du; = 2arcosh u + C; = 2arcosh (x − 2) + C.]

items.title: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arctangent Integral

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the denominator: [MATH: \eqalign{ 4x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 4x)\[5pt] & = -(x^2 - 2\cdot 2x + 2^2-2^2)\[5pt] & = -((x-2)^2 - 4) \[5pt] &= 4 - (x-2)^2 }]

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{4x-x^2}\textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{4-(x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x-2)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x-2).] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore, [MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − ((1)/(2)(x − 2))^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2})du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ artanh u + C; = (1)/(2)artanh ((x − 2)/(2)) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|\dfrac {x-2} {2} \right| < 1.]

Item 11 — Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arctangent Integral

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{4x-x^2} \textrm{d}x=]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:
[MATH: \eqalign{
4x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 4x)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 - 2\cdot 2x + 2^2-2^2)\[5pt]
& = -((x-2)^2 - 4) \[5pt]
&= 4 - (x-2)^2
}]

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{4x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x =
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x-2)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x-2).] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,
[MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − ((1)/(2)(x − 2))^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2})du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ artanh u + C; = (1)/(2)artanh ((x − 2)/(2)) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|\dfrac {x-2} {2} \right| < 1.]
